sections.h2: Who bills and collects property tax
sections.html:
Value and billing sit in different offices. The assessor decides what your property is worth and how it is classified. Payment goes to the treasurer at the Government Center. General questions go to the tax information line, 612-348-3011, which answers weekdays until 4:30, or to taxinfo@hennepin.us.

Every Hennepin County parcel sits inside several taxing districts at once, usually the county, a city, a school district and some special districts. More than 70 local governments levy on property here, and the auditor turns each levy and the assessment data into a rate for each district. The bill on your statement is the sum of all those pieces, so a house in one city can carry a very different bill from a similar house a few miles away.

sections.h2: Hennepin County housing at a glance
sections.html: Hennepin is Minnesota's most populous county, with 1,284,784 residents in the July 2025 estimate. About 62.7% of homes are owner occupied, the median owner-occupied home value is $392,900, and there are 587,984 housing units. The county holds 22 school districts, including Minneapolis, Edina, Minnetonka, Wayzata, Osseo Area and Anoka-Hennepin, and the district a house sits in is part of its tax bill. A seller in Hopkins or Maple Grove deals with different local rules than one in north Minneapolis, so start with the city on your statement.

Hennepin splits the bill into a May 15 payment and an October 15 payment. If a date falls on a weekend or holiday, you have until the next business day. These match the state rule in Minnesota Statutes 279.01 for any parcel with more than $100 in tax.

Pay late and the charge starts the very next day: 2 percent for a homestead, 4 percent for everything else. It doubles on the first of the following month, and each month after that through December adds 1 percent more. The ceiling is 8 percent for a homestead and 12 percent for a nonhomestead parcel. The county credits a late payment to penalty before it credits tax.

There is one way out. You can ask for a penalty abatement on a late half once every ten years, but only after the whole tax is paid and only if no older year is unpaid on the parcel.

Online payment is open for real property. You can use e-check, credit or debit card, PayPal and Venmo, and a payment counts as made the day it is submitted. Mobile home and personal property accounts have to use another method.

  • E-check costs nothing and is capped at $50,000 per transaction.
  • Cards, PayPal and Venmo are capped at $25,000 per transaction. Visa debit adds a $2.95 flat fee and other electronic methods add 2.29%. The county keeps none of it.
  • In person, on the 6th floor of the Government Center at 300 South 6th Street, weekdays 8 a.m. to 4:30 p.m. Card payments at the counter carry a 2.49% service fee.
  • A drop box on the same floor takes checks payable to Hennepin County Treasurer, weekdays from 6 a.m. to 6 p.m.
  • By phone at 1-877-626-0017, or by mail to the Hennepin County Treasurer at A-600 Government Center, Minneapolis, MN 55487-0060, postmarked on or before the due date.

Direct payment withdraws from a bank account on May 15 and October 15. Enrollment forms must arrive by April 15 for the first half and September 15 for the second.

The assessor assigns a market value as of January 2 each year and mails valuation notices in March. Every property is physically reviewed once every five years. The value you see now drives the tax you pay the next year, so read a notice that looks too high closely.

Start with a phone call to the assessor named on your notice, or attend an open book meeting if your city holds one. Still unhappy? Send a letter or appear at the local board of appeal and equalization, then take it to the county board in mid-June. To get on the county board's list, call 612-348-7050 or email countyvalueappeal@hennepin.us before the date shown on the notice. Court is the other path: Minnesota Tax Court, or a district court petition that Minnesota Statutes 278.01 requires by April 30 of the year the tax is payable.

sections.h2: Which cities run their own assessor?
sections.html:
Six cities handle assessment themselves, and an owner there calls the city instead of the county. Everywhere else the county assessor at 612-348-3046 answers the question.

  • Bloomington, 952-563-8722
  • Brooklyn Park, 763-493-8175
  • Eden Prairie, 952-949-8511
  • Minneapolis, 612-673-3000
  • Minnetonka, 952-939-8220
  • St. Louis Park, 952-924-2535

Calling the wrong office wastes the spring window, so check the notice mailed to the property before you dial.

Back taxes must be paid off before a deed can be recorded. Under Minnesota Statutes 272.12 the auditor reviews every deed headed for transfer, and the recorder will not take it without the auditor's note that nothing delinquent is outstanding. The recording checklist says the same thing in plain words.

This year's bill works differently. Splitting off a piece of a parcel calls for a treasurer's certification under Statutes 272.121 that the whole parcel's current tax is paid. For an ordinary sale of the whole lot, your title company decides how the year gets divided between you and the buyer. Request a county payoff figure if a half is still open. For an inherited house or one several years behind, ask for the payoff early so no surprise number stalls closing.

sections.h2: Homestead and ways to lower the bill
sections.html:
Homestead status is the main lever. To qualify you need a Social Security or individual taxpayer identification number, ownership in your own name instead of a business entity, and either you or a relative living in the home. A homesteaded property can qualify for a reduced classification rate, a reduced taxable market value and the state property tax refund.

Owners who just bought should check the taxpayer name and mailing address on the county property map and send a change form if either is wrong. The Property Watch email service tells an owner whenever a document is recorded against the parcel, which is useful when a payoff or release from an old loan is supposed to be recorded.

faqs.q: What are the Hennepin County property tax due dates?
faqs.a: The first half is due May 15 and the second October 15. A weekend or holiday moves the date to the next business day, and a mailed check needs a postmark by the due date.

faqs.q: Can I sell my Hennepin County house if the property taxes are unpaid?
faqs.a: Yes, once the back taxes are paid. A deed cannot be recorded until the auditor confirms nothing is delinquent, so the payoff usually comes out of the sale proceeds.

faqs.q: How do I contest my Hennepin County valuation?
faqs.a: Begin with the assessor named on your March notice, then go to the local board or the county board of appeal and equalization. The county board takes requests at 612-348-7050 or countyvalueappeal@hennepin.us until the date on the notice.

faqs.q: Does Hennepin County charge a fee to pay by card?
faqs.a: Yes, except for e-check, which is free online. Visa debit carries a flat $2.95 and other electronic methods 2.29%, and all of it goes to the processor. At the counter, cards cost 2.49%.

faqs.q: Who do I call with a Hennepin County property tax question?
faqs.a: Property tax information answers at 612-348-3011 and taxinfo@hennepin.us on weekdays. Questions about value go to the assessor at 612-348-3046, unless your city runs its own assessment.
